Three ways of asking|<div class=\"mxs\">:
CKA

Pick any two residues. Does each model think they are alike to the same degree — across every pair at once?

High = the two models rank resemblance the same way.

SVCCA

Each model spreads residues along a few main directions. Are those directions the same ones?

High = the same underlying axes, even if points sit differently along them.

mutual k-NN

Take a residue and list its 10 closest neighbours in each model. How many appear on both lists?

High = the two maps agree about what sits next to what.

the exception

Fold type is a shape category — and the model that has never seen a shape predicts it better than the model that has seen nothing else (0.685 vs 0.489). Evolutionary constraint, visible in sequence, carries information about fold and function at least as directly as this structure model's view of geometry does.

Macro-F1; intervals are the spread across five independent refits. The sequence model has 13 layers to pick its best from and the structure model 3, which favours sequence — the gaps here are far larger than that can explain, but the absolute numbers are optimistic for both. Six further properties were tested and are excluded because their intervals overlap or their baselines do nothing but guess the commonest answer.

The structure model already knows the geometry at its very first layer — it is handed the coordinates, so there is nothing to build. The sequence model has to construct that knowledge, climbing steadily with depth and never quite arriving. For function it is the reverse: the sequence model rises far above the amino-acid-counting baseline, while the structure model stays near it.
